title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero punishes the Christians after the fire of Rome (Church and Brodribb translation)
authors: Tacitus (trans. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: Nero fastened the guilt and inflicted the most exquisite tortures on a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace.
summary: Tacitus says Nero, to quell the belief that the Great Fire of AD 64 was ordered, put the blame on a group the populace called Christians. It is the earliest pagan description of Nero's punishment of Christians, written about 50 years after the event.
limits: The Latin form (Chrestianos as first written in the manuscript, later corrected) and the authenticity and historicity debates are in the caution candidates below. This is a 19th-c. English translation, not a critical Latin edition.

text.edition: Church and Brodribb translation (Perseus; Random House 1942 reprint of the 19th-c. translation)

title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Christus, Pilatus and the 'mischievous superstition'
authors: Tacitus (trans. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius
summary: Tacitus places the founder 'Christus' under Tiberius and the procurator Pontius Pilatus, and says the 'mischievous superstition' broke out again in Judaea, 'the first source of the evil', and then in Rome. He names no source for this.
limits: Tacitus says 'procurator' where the Pilate Stone points to 'prefect'; scholars read this as Tacitus' anachronism, and a few as a sign of interpolation (see the Tacitus on Jesus candidate). The passage shows what an elite Roman historian believed c. 115, not independent evidence about Jesus.

title: Tacitus, Histories 5.2: competing accounts of Jewish origins
authors: Tacitus (trans. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: Others, again, assign a very distinguished origin to the Jews, alleging that they were the Solymi, a nation celebrated in the poems of Homer
summary: Tacitus lists several origin stories (Cretan fugitives, Egyptian emigrants led by Hierosolymus and Judas, Ethiopians, Assyrians, Homeric Solymi) without choosing one, introducing them as he 'is about to relate the last days of a famous city'.
limits: These are Roman reports, not Jewish self-description, and none matches the Hebrew Bible's account. They are claims Tacitus records, not demonstrated routes.

title: Tacitus, Histories 5.5: Jewish customs, 'hatred of enemies' and monotheism
authors: Tacitus (trans. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: among themselves they are inflexibly honest and ever ready to shew compassion, though they regard the rest of mankind with all the hatred of enemies.
summary: In the same chapter Tacitus says Jews have 'purely mental conceptions of Deity, as one in essence' and no images, and that proselytes are taught to 'despise all gods, to disown their country'. He pairs real knowledge (aniconism, circumcision, burial) with a hostile frame.
limits: A hostile Roman senator's characterisation, not a neutral ethnography. The claim that Jewish burial follows 'the Egyptian custom' is Tacitus' own and is not shown to be a transfer. Same dating and manuscript limits as other Histories entries.

title: Tacitus, Histories 5.13: the siege omens and the Eastern prophecy
authors: Tacitus (trans. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: in the ancient records of their priests was contained a prediction of how at this very time the East was to grow powerful
summary: Tacitus reports prodigies at the temple and a belief that rulers 'coming from Judaea' would acquire universal empire, a prophecy he says pointed to Vespasian and Titus; he also gives the besieged as 600,000 ('I have heard').
limits: Tacitus relays the prediction second-hand and applies it to the Flavians; it is a Roman reading of Jewish expectation, and the 600,000 figure is hearsay. Josephus is a parallel but was not opened here.

title: Suetonius, Claudius 25.4: Jews expelled 'at the instigation of Chrestus'
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus
summary: Suetonius records, undated, a Claudian expulsion of Jews from Rome after disturbances connected with 'Chrestus' (Latin impulsore Chresto). It sits in a topical list, so the date has to come from other sources (Orosius gives AD 49; Dio 60.6.6 reports no expulsion).
limits: Whether Chrestus is Jesus (a spelling of Christus), an otherwise unknown agitator, or someone else is disputed (see the Chrestus candidates). The Latin is ambiguous on whether all Jews or only the agitators were expelled.

text.edition: J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library, 1914 (public domain; transcription by B. Thayer, LacusCurtius/Penelope)

title: Suetonius, Nero 16.2: punishment of the Christians
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: Punishment was inflicted on the Christians, a class of men given to a new and mischievous superstition.
summary: Suetonius lists the punishment of Christians among Nero's regulatory acts, with no mention of the fire of Rome. It agrees with Tacitus on 'mischievous superstition' (superstitio) but not on the occasion.
limits: A one-line item in a list of reforms; it neither confirms nor denies the arson-scapegoat story. Tacitus and Suetonius wrote within a few years of each other, and whether Suetonius is independent of Tacitus was not established from the pages opened.

title: Cassius Dio 60.6.6: Claudius bars Jewish meetings but does not expel them
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions; Chrestus identification
quote: he did not drive them out, but ordered them, while continuing their traditional mode of life, not to hold meetings.
summary: Dio places an action against Jews early in Claudius' reign and says he did not drive them out because they were too numerous, only forbade assemblies. This stands against the expulsion in Suetonius and Orosius.
limits: Dio and Suetonius may describe different measures (AD 41 versus c. 49) or one event differently; the passage does not mention Chrestus or Christians.

title: Cassius Dio 69.12: Aelia Capitolina and the cause of the Jewish revolt under Hadrian
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions (Dio 69.12-14)
quote: At Jerusalem he founded a city in place of the one which had been razed to the ground, naming it Aelia Capitolina
summary: Dio gives the founding of Aelia Capitolina and a temple of Jupiter on the temple site as the cause of a 'war of no slight importance', in which Jews fortified positions with mines and walls.
limits: Dio's causal account is one of several in modern scholarship; this entry does not resolve it. Dio never names Bar Kokhba in these chapters, so the link to the revolt of 132-135 rests on other sources. Book 69 survives only via Xiphilinus' epitome.

title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 5.73: the Essenes west of the Dead Sea
authors: Pliny the Elder (trans. J. Bostock and H. T. Riley)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions
quote: a people that live apart from the world, and marvellous beyond all others throughout the whole earth, for they have no women among them
summary: Pliny places the Essenes west of Lake Asphaltites and describes them as celibate and moneyless, recruited by newcomers 'wearied with the miseries of life'; En-gedi, below them, is 'now ... a heap of ashes'.
limits: Written within a decade of the war and dedicated to Titus; Pliny probably drew on a literary source. The passage does not tie the Essenes to Qumran or to Christianity; those links are modern inferences. Perseus numbers follow Bostock-Riley, not the modern 5.73 divisions.

text.edition: J. Bostock and H. T. Riley, Taylor and Francis, London, 1855 (Perseus)

title: Philo, Against Flaccus 55: Alexandrian Jews confined to one quarter (38 CE)
authors: Philo of Alexandria (trans. C. D. Yonge)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions (Philo, Against Flaccus)
quote: They drove the Jews entirely out of four quarters, and crammed them all into a very small portion of one
summary: Philo, an Alexandrian Jew, says the Roman prefect Flaccus issued an edict calling Jews 'foreigners and aliens', after which the mob drove them from four of Alexandria's five districts into one and looted their shops.
limits: Philo is a Jewish partisan writing about the persecution of his own community, and Flaccus is not a Roman historian; the brief names it expressly. Composition date is a loose inference (see basis).

title: Philo, Embassy to Gaius 155-156: the Jews of Rome beyond the Tiber
authors: Philo of Alexandria (trans. C. D. Yonge)
ask_addressed: Quote Roman and Greek historians on Jews and Christians from open editions (Philo, Embassy to Gaius)
quote: And they were mostly Roman citizens, having been emancipated; for, having been brought as captives into Italy, they were manumitted
summary: Philo describes a large Jewish quarter across the Tiber, mostly freedpeople and citizens, with synagogues, sabbath gatherings and temple tithes sent to Jerusalem, tolerated by Augustus; it is evidence for the community Claudius later disturbed.
limits: Philo writes to praise Augustan policy and to nudge Claudius, so the picture is shaped for an argument. He mentions neither Chrestus nor any Christian group.

title: The Myth of the Neronian Persecution
ask_addressed: Composition dates with basis, earliest manuscript witness, and scholarly cautions (Tacitus authenticity debate, Chrestus identification)
quote: The only source for this event is a brief passage in the historian Tacitus.
summary: Shaw argues that there was no state persecution of Christians under Nero after the fire and that Tacitus' account reflects ideas of his own day (c. 115). His abstract says the passage is 'probably genuine Tacitus', so the challenge is to historicity, not authorship.
limits: Only the abstract and reference list opened (full text behind access). The abstract shows the debate is not about interpolation.

title: The Historicity of the Neronian Persecution: A Response to Brent Shaw
ask_addressed: Composition dates with basis, earliest manuscript witness, and scholarly cautions (Tacitus authenticity debate, Chrestus identification)
quote: In fact, there are no grounds for doubting Tacitus’ report of the persecution.
summary: Jones answers Shaw and defends Tacitus' report. He argues that Chrestiani is not an anachronism, citing Acts 11.26 (Christianoi called first at Antioch) and the -ianus suffix as a hostile outsiders' name.
limits: Jones separates Tacitus' report from the later tradition that Peter and Paul died in it. Both sides accept the passage as Tacitean, so this does not test the interpolation theory.

title: The Historicity of the Neronian Persecution (on the manuscript reading Chrestiani)
ask_addressed: Composition dates with basis, earliest manuscript witness, and scholarly cautions (Tacitus authenticity debate, Chrestus identification)
quote: In the only manuscript, the second Medicean, Chrestiani appears to have been changed to Christiani by a later hand
summary: Jones reports that Annals 15.44's group name stands as Chrestiani in the sole witness and was later altered, bearing on the Chrestus/Christus spelling question and on how thinly the text is transmitted.
limits: A scholar's description of the manuscript, not a collation; no image of the folio was opened. Whether the earlier spelling is Tacitus' or a scribe's is not settled by this sentence.
